summary: A proposed Telnet protocol from the committee, circulated before the Atlantic City meeting. Telnet lets a user at one computer log in to another across the network as if directly attached. It was meant to give early implementers a common basis and was not final. RFC 139 gives background and RFC 158 revised it.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal describes how a user at one host can interact with a process at another host through Telnet. It defines a shared terminal format so hosts do not need to exchange details about every local terminal.

subtitle: A proposed 1971 Telnet protocol based on a shared virtual terminal for remote access.

tldr.problem: Different hosts and terminals had different conventions, and each host should not need to track every other host's characteristics.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines a Network Virtual Terminal using ASCII data and separate control signals for features such as break and echo.
tldr.outcome: The document was circulated as a proposal for review and early implementation. It was updated by RFC 139.

sections.title: Purpose and Proposal Status
sections.content:
This document was circulated before the Atlantic City meetings for review and discussion. It was intended to give installations planning early Telnet implementations a common basis. The author says it represents a protocol the committee considered adequate for initial implementation, with some suggestions not yet cleared by all members.

Telnet is described as a third-level protocol that makes a terminal or process at a using site appear to the serving site as if it were directly connected there. It aims to minimize how much each host must know about other hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a proposal for early Telnet implementations, not a final specification. It describes how one host can provide remote access through a shared terminal format.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
Telnet provides a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT). Its data uses seven-bit ASCII sent in eight-bit bytes with the high-order bit set to zero. The using site must let users produce all ASCII codes and a set of Telnet control signals.

The serving site specifies how NVT codes map to its local terminal. The proposal represents the end of a line as carriage return followed by line feed and assumes that the serving site initially provides no echo.
sections.plainLanguage: The two hosts exchange data using a shared set of ASCII conventions. Each host translates between those conventions and its own terminal.

sections.title: Telnet Control Signals
sections.content:
Telnet control signals use eight-bit codes with the high-order bit set to one. The codes listed include a data-type signal for ASCII, break or attention, reverse break, echo directions, a not-implemented notice and a return-to-control-mode signal. Two code values are reserved.

Some local signals do not need a code sent over the network: transmitting all data so far and suppressing end-of-line transmission while sending other data. The RFC says this document may be revised to provide conventions for additional data types.
sections.plainLanguage: Bytes with the high bit set carry control signals rather than ordinary ASCII data. The proposal lists signals for break, echo and changes between data and control modes.
